issues.issue: "Damaged cards will be replaced free of charge, but there is a fee to replace a lost card" leaves unclear which rule governs a card that is both lost and later returned damaged. The boundary between "lost" and "damaged" is not defined.

The enumerated privileges (check cashing, elections, athletic events, library, campus technologies) are followed by "etc.", leaving the reach of the catch-all uncertain, and "properly entitled" is nowhere defined. A student and the University could reasonably differ on what falls inside the list.

"Encouraging, enticing, influencing, or enlisting" another student is undefined, and "influencing" in particular has no ascertainable boundary. Ordinary conversation could fall within it on one reading.

"Maintain currency with the use of the University-issued e-mail account" states no frequency or standard, and the following sentence ("communicating information important requests, updates") is garbled by a missing word or punctuation. What the student actually must do is therefore uncertain.

This provision underpins the notice mechanism in Section 19.1 and 19.6 (charges and hearing notice delivered to the Brandeis e-mail account), but it imposes no clear duty that would make such delivery effective notice.

The prohibited behaviours are listed as bare verbs — "intimidates", "threatens", "harasses or bullies", "invades personal privacy", "unwanted physical contact", "endangers the health, safety, or welfare" — with no definitions or intent element. These are the charging standards for discipline and each is reasonably susceptible of narrow and broad readings.

The final sentence permits emergency suspension of any student "involved in such an incident" pending investigation, while Section 22.2 permits altering a student's status only for "reasons of imminent danger". The two cannot easily be read together.

A duty to "comply with instructions of University officials, committees, or boards" is unlimited in subject matter and contains no reasonableness or scope qualifier. Whether it reaches any instruction whatever is genuinely open.
"Dean's Action" is used here as a defined-sounding term but Section 22 speaks of "Dean's Actions and Sanctions" without defining "Dean's Action" as such. The referent is left to inference.

"Obstructing or disrupting ... administrative, public service, disciplinary, or other authorized functions" ends in an open catch-all whose reach beyond the enumerated functions is uncertain. "Legitimate functions" is itself undefined.

"Causes disruption to" and "invades another individual's privacy" are undefined and the sentence's grammar leaves it unclear whether "in a classroom, library or other campus facility" qualifies both verbs. The scope of the prohibition therefore shifts with the reading.

"Issuing any type of threat" is appended to a provision otherwise about safety equipment and is unlimited in scope. Its placement makes it unclear whether it is confined to safety-related threats or free-standing.

The protected categories listed here differ from those listed in Sections 7.0, 7.1 and 7.3 (which add ancestry, religious creed, veteran status categories and "any other category protected by law"). The inconsistent lists leave the covered classes uncertain.

Hazing is "defined" as "initiating or disciplining fellow students, often in the nature of forced alcohol consumption, humiliating or painful ordeals" — the word "often" makes the examples non-limiting so the definition covers any initiation or discipline of a fellow student. The operative boundary of the offense is not ascertainable from the text.

After a list of specific weapons the clause sweeps in "other articles or substances usable as weapons", a catch-all that on its face captures ordinary objects such as kitchen knives or tools. Whether ejusdem generis confines it to weapon-like items is exactly the kind of question a court is asked.

The first sentence bars bringing "any dog or animal" onto campus "without a leash", which read literally requires leashing every animal, while the second sentence exempts guide and service animals only from certain buildings. The two sentences leave the actual rule uncertain.

The host assumes responsibility for "the actions, damage, or injuries caused by" a guest without any limit of foreseeability or fault. Whether this creates strict liability for all guest conduct is genuinely open.

The clause incorporates "regulations enumerated in other official University publications and documents" with only illustrative examples ("e.g."), so the body of incorporated rules is not identified. What documents bind the student is left at large.

The prohibition reaches behaviour that "could be construed as retaliation", a standard defined by how a third party might perceive it rather than by conduct or intent. Its boundary cannot be applied without construction.

The section says non-consensual interaction "could be defined as sexual misconduct or sexual assault" without defining either term, and requires consent to be "sought and clearly understood and communicated" without saying by what measure. This is the charging standard and its terms are left open.

The statement that any student "accused" of sexual misconduct may be placed on emergency suspension pending investigation cannot be squared with Section 22.2, which forbids altering a student's status pending final action except for "imminent danger".

"Sexual misconduct" is prohibited but never defined; the section says only that non-consensual "sexual contact" "may be considered" misconduct, and "sexual contact" is likewise undefined. Whether particular conduct is an offense turns on words the document never fixes.

This section requires "explicit consent" that is "clearly communicated", while Section 3.3 provides that consent "may be communicated verbally or through actions" and may be inferred. The two consent standards point in different directions.

"Taking advantage of someone's incapacitation or intoxication" makes mere intoxication — not incapacity — sufficient, whereas the same sentence treats the two as interchangeable. "Taking advantage of" has no defined content.

Section 3.1 provides that only a student who is "physically or mentally incapacitated" cannot consent, while this section makes sexual activity with a merely "intoxicated" person misconduct. The two provisions set different thresholds.

Lack of consent may be inferred from incapacity "of which the Accused was aware or should have been aware", an objective standard nowhere elaborated, and consent may be shown "through actions". Both formulations are open to competing readings in a disciplinary charge.
Permitting consent to be communicated "through actions" is difficult to reconcile with Section 3.1's requirement of "explicit consent" that is "clearly communicated".

This summary says the Advisor must come "from the University community" and that counsel may give only "passive assistance", but the Advisor definition in Section 22.6 says that where criminal proceedings coexist "the Advisor role may instead be held by a party's attorney". The two descriptions of the right to counsel differ.

"Work that is falsified or is not the result of the student's own effort" is the operative prohibition, and "own effort" is not defined against permitted collaboration or tutoring. The line between a "quality of work" concern and an "integrity" concern is likewise left to the department.

The provision ends mid-sentence ("Talking during an examination, or possession or use of"), so the prohibition it was stating is incomplete. What is forbidden cannot be determined from the text as written.
"Appropriate posting materials that will not cause damage" fixes no standard and is judged only after the fact. A student cannot tell in advance what materials qualify.

The Department may remove chalked messages that are "inappropriate" or use "profane illustrations or language", terms given no content. "Only sidewalks may be chalked" also sits awkwardly against the separate prohibition on areas rain cannot wash.
"Inappropriate use of property" and the extension to "personal and public property that surrounds the campus" have no defined limit. How far beyond campus the section reaches is genuinely uncertain.
"Mistreatment of animals, trees, or plantings" is undefined and covers everything from cruelty to picking a flower. The standard cannot be applied without construction.

The policy prohibits discrimination on the basis of listed categories "or any other category protected by law", an open-ended addition to a specific list whose reach is uncertain. The categories also differ from those enumerated in Sections 2.7 and 7.3.

The "Note" routing all Section 7 allegations to the Special Examiner's Process is difficult to square with Section 19.10.C's "Rights to Fairness" statement, which promises rights (questioning witnesses, presenting witnesses) that the Special Examiner's Process does not provide.

Conduct is "harassment" when it has "the purpose or effect of unreasonably interfering" or creates an "intimidating, hostile or offensive environment", judged without any objective-reasonableness anchor. Whether a subjective sense of offense suffices is left open.

The list of sexual-harassment examples is expressly non-exhaustive ("includes, but is not limited to") and prefaced by "Depending on the circumstances", so nothing on the list is necessarily a violation and nothing off it is necessarily permitted. The list's operative effect is uncertain.

The section states the examples are "not an exhaustive list" and then reserves the right to act on conduct the University "deems to be inappropriate, regardless of whether it rises to the level of a violation of law". The prohibited conduct is therefore bounded only by the University's own judgment.

Section 2.14 forbids conduct that "could be construed as retaliation", while this section prohibits retaliation against a person who "in good faith" complains or cooperates. The two formulations of the same prohibition differ in scope.
"Falsified a claim" is not defined and does not distinguish a knowingly false report from an unsubstantiated one. Who makes that determination, and by what standard, is not stated.

"Malicious or unauthorized entry into ... personal files, electronic files ... or locked spaces, such as lockers, etc." ends in an undefined catch-all, and "entry" into electronic files is not explained. The reach of the prohibition is left open.

The section excepts "circumstances as outlined in Section 10.5", a section not reproduced in this instrument, so the scope of the exception to the search-permission requirement cannot be determined from the document.

Reports must be submitted "in a timely manner" and a case may be refused if "not reported in a timely fashion", with no period stated. The limitation period is left entirely to the administrator's judgment.

This section says disciplinary action "may be implemented only through the report of a violation to the DSRCS", yet Sections 22.1, 22.3 and 22.4 permit the Dean to remove, suspend or sanction a student without any such report. The word "only" cannot be reconciled with those powers.

The outcome of mediation is said to be "agreed-upon, recorded, final, and binding" while "the Director must also approve all proposed resolutions", so whether the parties or the Director controls the outcome is unclear. "Final and binding" is also unqualified as to further conduct action.

A mediated outcome is described as "final, and binding", but Section 18.2 provides that failure to adhere to it may expose the party to "further mediation or referral to the conduct process". The finality is thus contradicted.

This section allows referral of a defaulting party to the conduct process, which sits against Section 18.1's statement that a mediated resolution is "final, and binding". Whether a mediated outcome forecloses conduct charges is left unresolved.

Failure to choose an option within 2 business days "constitutes an acceptance of responsibility for the violation", a deemed admission with no notice or hardship qualification other than unspecified "extenuating circumstances". The trigger and the escape hatch are both left to the administrator.

The section directs the administrator to "proceed to sanctioning in accordance with Section 19.3", but Section 19.3 addresses only a student's failure to attend a scheduled Administrative Action meeting and prescribes no sanctioning procedure. The cross-reference points nowhere.

The meeting is described as "the only opportunity to present evidence", yet the same sentence says it may be "waived in the event of" the Preliminary Meeting, leaving open whether a student who has had a Preliminary Meeting gets any evidentiary opportunity at all.
"Pending charges may be discontinued thereafter dependent upon the conduct of the Accused" states no criterion and no decision-maker. What conduct produces discontinuance cannot be determined.
